title: Health, Disease & Immunity
description: What causes disease — pathogens, transmission, the immune system, antibiotics, vaccination, and how lifestyle affects health.

notes.heading: What is Disease? Pathogens and Transmission
notes.body: A disease is any condition that impairs the normal functioning of an organism. Communicable (infectious) diseases are caused by pathogens and can be transmitted between individuals. Non-communicable diseases (e.g., heart disease, cancer, diabetes) are not infectious — they have genetic, lifestyle, or environmental causes. The four types of pathogens: (1) Bacteria — unicellular prokaryotes. Examples of diseases: cholera (Vibrio cholerae — water contaminated with faeces), tuberculosis (Mycobacterium tuberculosis — airborne droplets), food poisoning (Salmonella — contaminated food). (2) Viruses — much smaller than bacteria; not cells — they invade host cells and use the cell's machinery to replicate. Examples: influenza (airborne droplets), HIV (blood/sexual contact), common cold, COVID-19. (3) Fungi — examples: athlete's foot, ringworm (both spread by direct contact). (4) Protists (protozoa) — eukaryotic single-celled parasites. Example: malaria (Plasmodium — spread by female Anopheles mosquito vectors). Transmission routes: airborne (droplets from coughs/sneezes), waterborne (contaminated water), foodborne (undercooked/contaminated food), direct contact (touching infected person or surfaces), vector-borne (carried by another organism e.g., mosquito, tick), sexual contact, blood-to-blood.

illustration.alt: Diagram showing the four types of pathogens and the routes by which infectious diseases spread.
illustration.caption: Bacteria, viruses, fungi, and protists cause communicable diseases; pathogens travel by air, water, food, contact, vectors, and body fluids.

notes.heading: The Body's First Line of Defence (Non-Specific Barriers)
notes.body: The human body has physical and chemical barriers that prevent most pathogens from entering — these are non-specific (work against ALL pathogens, not specific types). (1) Skin — tough outer layer of dead keratinised cells; a physical barrier. Sebum (oil) on skin contains antimicrobial substances. (2) Mucus and cilia — airways are lined with mucus-secreting cells that trap pathogens and particles. Ciliated epithelial cells sweep the mucus upwards to the throat where it is swallowed — stomach acid then destroys the trapped pathogens. (3) Stomach acid — hydrochloric acid (pH ~1-2) kills most ingested bacteria and pathogens. (4) Tears — contain lysozyme, an enzyme that breaks down bacterial cell walls. (5) Blood clotting — if skin is broken, platelets trigger a clotting cascade that seals the wound, preventing pathogen entry. (6) The inflammatory response — damaged tissue releases histamine, causing blood vessels to dilate (redness, swelling). This increases blood flow, bringing white blood cells to the site of infection.

illustration.alt: Diagram of the human body showing non-specific physical and chemical barriers against pathogens.
illustration.caption: Skin, mucus and cilia, stomach acid, tears, blood clotting, and inflammation form the first line of defence.

notes.heading: The Immune System (Specific Defence)
notes.body: If pathogens breach the non-specific barriers, the specific immune response is activated. White blood cells (leukocytes) are the key players: (1) Phagocytes (e.g., macrophages, neutrophils) — carry out phagocytosis: they engulf and digest pathogens. They are non-specific — they attack any foreign cell. Process: phagocyte detects pathogen → extends pseudopodia to surround it → engulfs it into a phagosome → enzymes digest the pathogen. (2) Lymphocytes (B cells and T cells) — the specific defence. Each B lymphocyte produces antibodies specific to one particular antigen (a protein marker on the pathogen surface). Antibodies bind to antigens, neutralising the pathogen or marking it for destruction by phagocytes. After an infection, memory lymphocytes remain in the body for years or even a lifetime. If the same pathogen invades again, memory cells rapidly produce antibodies before the pathogen can cause illness — this is immunity. The primary response (first infection) is slow (symptoms appear). The secondary response (subsequent exposure) is fast and strong (no symptoms). This is the basis of vaccination.

illustration.alt: Diagram showing phagocytosis and antibodies produced by lymphocytes binding to pathogen antigens.
illustration.caption: Phagocytes engulf pathogens non-specifically, while lymphocytes make specific antibodies and memory cells.

notes.heading: Vaccination (Immunisation)
notes.body: Vaccination induces artificial active immunity without causing the disease. How it works: (1) A vaccine contains a weakened (attenuated), inactivated (dead), or fragment of a pathogen — or just the pathogen's antigen. (2) The vaccine is injected or taken orally. (3) The immune system recognises the foreign antigen and mounts a primary response: lymphocytes produce antibodies and memory cells. (4) If the person is later exposed to the actual pathogen, memory cells recognise it and rapidly produce large quantities of antibodies — the secondary response prevents illness. Examples: MMR vaccine (measles, mumps, rubella), polio vaccine, HPV vaccine (protects against cervical cancer-causing virus), COVID-19 vaccines. Herd immunity: when a high percentage (~95%) of a population is vaccinated, the pathogen cannot spread easily. This protects those who cannot be vaccinated (infants, immunocompromised individuals, elderly). This is why vaccination is a public health measure, not just a personal choice. Common misconception: vaccines do NOT give you the disease — the pathogen is either dead or weakened to the point of being harmless.

illustration.alt: Diagram showing a vaccine triggering a primary immune response and memory cells for a faster secondary response.
illustration.caption: A vaccine triggers antibodies and memory cells without causing disease, so later infection is stopped quickly.

notes.heading: Antibiotics and Antiseptics
notes.body: Antibiotics are medicines that kill or inhibit the growth of bacteria (NOT viruses, NOT fungi, NOT protists). They work by targeting bacterial-specific structures or processes: disrupting cell wall synthesis (e.g., penicillin — bacteria burst without cell wall; human cells have no cell wall, so are unaffected), inhibiting protein synthesis by targeting bacterial ribosomes (which differ from human ribosomes), or interfering with bacterial DNA replication. Important facts: (1) Antibiotics do NOT work against viruses (common cold, flu, COVID-19 are viral and should not be treated with antibiotics). (2) Antibiotic resistance — a major global health crisis. When a population of bacteria is exposed to antibiotics, most die but some may have random mutations conferring resistance. These survive, reproduce, and pass on resistance genes. Over time, the antibiotic becomes ineffective. Causes: overuse and misuse of antibiotics (e.g., prescribing for viral infections), patients not completing their course (leaving partially resistant bacteria alive). MRSA (Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus) is a dangerous example of antibiotic-resistant bacteria. Antiseptics (e.g., alcohol, iodine, hydrogen peroxide) are chemicals applied to living tissue to kill or inhibit microorganisms. Disinfectants are similar but used on non-living surfaces. Both reduce spread but are external — they do NOT cure infections inside the body.

illustration.alt: Diagram comparing antibiotics bursting bacteria, having no effect on viruses, and antiseptics acting on skin.
illustration.caption: Antibiotics target bacterial structures, do not affect viruses, and overuse drives antibiotic resistance.

notes.heading: Lifestyle and Non-Communicable Disease
notes.body: Non-communicable diseases (NCDs) are not caused by pathogens and cannot be transmitted. They are the leading cause of death globally. Major risk factors: (1) Diet — high saturated fat and cholesterol increases risk of cardiovascular disease (atherosclerosis — fatty plaques build up in arteries, narrowing them; can lead to heart attacks or strokes). High salt intake contributes to hypertension (high blood pressure). High sugar intake contributes to obesity and type 2 diabetes (body becomes resistant to insulin). (2) Smoking — tobacco contains carcinogens (cancer-causing chemicals); causes lung cancer, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), and cardiovascular disease. Tar damages cilia in airways; carbon monoxide reduces blood oxygen capacity; nicotine is addictive and increases heart rate. (3) Alcohol — excessive consumption damages the liver (cirrhosis), increases cancer risk, and can cause brain damage. (4) Lack of exercise — contributes to obesity, cardiovascular disease, and type 2 diabetes. (5) Genetics — some NCDs have genetic components (e.g., certain cancers, type 1 diabetes, cystic fibrosis). The interaction between genetics, lifestyle, and environment means NCDs are often multifactorial.

illustration.alt: Diagram showing lifestyle and genetic risk factors contributing to non-communicable diseases.
illustration.caption: Diet, smoking, alcohol, lack of exercise, and genetics all raise the risk of NCDs such as heart disease and diabetes.

notes.heading: Investigating Antimicrobials — Practical
notes.body: A classic practical uses agar plates to test the effectiveness of different antimicrobial substances: (1) Sterilise equipment and workspace (aseptic technique — prevents contamination). (2) Using a sterile spreader, spread a bacterial lawn evenly over the surface of a nutrient agar plate. (3) Use sterile forceps to place paper discs soaked in different antimicrobials (e.g., different antibiotics, antiseptics, or mouthwashes) onto the agar. Include a control disc with sterile water. (4) Incubate the plate upside down at 25°C for 24-48 hours (not 37°C — which would encourage human pathogens). (5) Measure the clear zone (zone of inhibition) around each disc — the larger the zone, the more effective the antimicrobial. (6) Calculate the area of the inhibition zone: Area = πr² (where r = radius of zone including the disc, OR zone width ÷ 2). Compare areas to determine relative effectiveness. Safety: do NOT open incubated plates — bacteria colonies can be pathogenic. Dispose by autoclaving. Variables: independent = type of antimicrobial; dependent = size of inhibition zone; controls = disc material, volume of antimicrobial, incubation time, temperature.

illustration.alt: Diagram of an agar plate with antimicrobial discs and clear zones of inhibition.
illustration.caption: Larger zones of inhibition around a disc mean the antimicrobial is more effective at stopping bacterial growth.

flashcards.definition: A microorganism that causes disease. Four types: bacteria, viruses, fungi, and protists (protozoa).
flashcards.example: Salmonella (bacteria — food poisoning), influenza virus (flu), Plasmodium (protist — malaria).

flashcards.definition: A non-specific immune response where phagocytes (white blood cells) engulf, enclose, and digest pathogens using enzymes.
flashcards.example: Macrophages patrol tissues and engulf any foreign bacteria they encounter.

flashcards.definition: A Y-shaped protein produced by B lymphocytes that binds specifically to an antigen on a pathogen, neutralising or marking it for destruction.
flashcards.example: Each antibody is specific — an antibody against the measles virus will not bind to the influenza virus.

flashcards.definition: A protein or other molecule on the surface of a pathogen that the immune system recognises as foreign, triggering an antibody response.
flashcards.example: Spike proteins on the surface of the COVID-19 virus are antigens recognised by the immune system.

flashcards.definition: A long-lived B or T cell that remains after an infection; enables rapid antibody production if the same pathogen invades again — the basis of immunity.
flashcards.example: After recovering from chickenpox, memory cells provide lifelong immunity — you rarely get it twice.

flashcards.definition: Introducing a weakened, dead, or fragmentary form of a pathogen to stimulate the immune system to produce memory cells without causing disease.
flashcards.example: The MMR vaccine contains weakened measles, mumps, and rubella viruses — triggering immunity to all three.

flashcards.definition: When a high proportion of a population is vaccinated, the pathogen cannot spread easily, protecting unvaccinated individuals.
flashcards.example: If 95% are vaccinated against measles, the virus cannot find enough susceptible hosts to sustain an outbreak.

flashcards.definition: A medicine that kills bacteria or stops them reproducing. Does NOT work against viruses, fungi, or protists.
flashcards.example: Penicillin disrupts bacterial cell wall synthesis. It is useless against viral infections like the common cold.

flashcards.definition: When bacteria evolve to survive exposure to an antibiotic; caused by overuse and misuse of antibiotics. Resistant bacteria survive, reproduce, and spread resistance genes.
flashcards.example: MRSA (Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus) is resistant to multiple antibiotics, making infections difficult to treat.

flashcards.definition: Methods used to prevent contamination when culturing microorganisms — sterilising equipment, using a Bunsen burner to create an updraft, flaming bottlenecks.
flashcards.example: In laboratory bacterial cultures, Petri dishes are incubated at 25°C (not 37°C) to reduce the risk of growing human pathogens.

flashcards.definition: A disease not caused by pathogens and not transmissible between people. Associated with lifestyle, genetics, and environmental factors.
flashcards.example: Type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, lung cancer (from smoking), and cirrhosis (from alcohol) are NCDs.

flashcards.definition: The clear area around an antibiotic/antimicrobial disc on an agar plate where bacteria have been killed or prevented from growing. Larger diameter = more effective.
flashcards.example: A disc of penicillin producing a 20 mm inhibition zone is more effective against the tested bacteria than one producing a 10 mm zone.

questions.stem: Which of these diseases is caused by a virus?
choices: Cholera (from contaminated water)
Athlete's foot (skin infection)
Influenza (flu)
Malaria
questions.explanation: Influenza is caused by the influenza virus. Cholera = bacteria (Vibrio cholerae), athlete's foot = fungus, malaria = protist (Plasmodium).

questions.stem: How do ciliated epithelial cells protect the respiratory system?
choices: They produce antibodies that kill pathogens
They secrete mucus that traps pathogens, then cilia sweep the mucus up to the throat to be swallowed
They form a waterproof barrier in the lungs
They produce stomach acid that kills bacteria
questions.explanation: Cilia are tiny hair-like projections that beat in coordinated waves, moving mucus (with trapped pathogens and particles) up to the throat. The mucus is swallowed and stomach acid destroys the pathogens.

questions.stem: What is the difference between a phagocyte and a lymphocyte?
choices: Phagocytes produce antibodies; lymphocytes engulf pathogens
Phagocytes engulf and digest pathogens non-specifically; lymphocytes produce specific antibodies and memory cells
They are the same type of cell with different names
Phagocytes work outside the body; lymphocytes work inside
questions.explanation: Phagocytes (macrophages, neutrophils) carry out phagocytosis — non-specific engulfing of any foreign material. Lymphocytes are specific — each one produces antibodies against a single antigen.

questions.stem: Why does a vaccine NOT make you ill from the disease it protects against?
choices: The vaccine contains antibiotics that kill the pathogen immediately
The vaccine contains weakened, dead, or fragmented pathogens that cannot cause disease but still trigger an immune response
The vaccine only works after you already have the disease
The vaccine contains memory cells, not pathogens
questions.explanation: Vaccines use attenuated (weakened), inactivated (dead), or subunit (fragments/antigens) forms of the pathogen. These cannot cause full disease but are enough to stimulate immunity and memory cell production.

questions.stem: A patient has flu-like symptoms. The doctor prescribes antibiotics. Why is this inappropriate?
choices: Antibiotics only work against bacteria — flu is caused by a virus, so antibiotics will have no effect and contribute to antibiotic resistance
Antibiotics are too expensive for viral infections
The patient should just rest instead
Antibiotics will make the virus mutate faster
questions.explanation: Antibiotics target bacterial-specific features (cell wall, ribosomes). Viruses have none of these — they use the host cell's machinery. Prescribing antibiotics for viral infections is ineffective and contributes to the antibiotic resistance crisis.

questions.stem: How does antibiotic resistance develop in a bacterial population?
choices: Bacteria choose to become resistant when they detect antibiotics
Random mutations produce resistance in a few bacteria; when exposed to antibiotics, these survive and reproduce, passing resistance genes — the population evolves
Antibiotics directly change bacterial DNA to become resistant
All bacteria are naturally resistant to all antibiotics
questions.explanation: Antibiotic resistance evolves through natural selection. Random mutations produce rare resistant individuals. Antibiotics kill susceptible bacteria, leaving resistant ones to thrive — these multiply and the resistance allele frequency increases.

questions.stem: A student tests three mouthwashes by placing soaked discs on a bacterial lawn. After incubation, Mouthwash A has a 12 mm inhibition zone, B has 20 mm, C has 5 mm. Which is most effective at killing bacteria?
choices: Mouthwash A
Mouthwash B
Mouthwash C
They are all equally effective
questions.explanation: The larger the zone of inhibition, the more effective the antimicrobial at killing or inhibiting bacterial growth. Mouthwash B (20 mm) is clearly the most effective in this test.

questions.stem: Why is aseptic technique important when culturing bacteria in the lab?
choices: To make the bacteria grow faster
To prevent contamination of the culture with unwanted microorganisms (including pathogens from the air/surfaces) and to prevent the cultured bacteria from escaping and causing harm
To save money on agar plates
To ensure the bacteria produce more toxins for study
questions.explanation: Aseptic technique (sterilising equipment, flaming bottlenecks, working near a Bunsen updraft) prevents contamination both ways — stops environmental microbes from growing on your plate and stops your cultured bacteria from escaping.

questions.stem: What is herd immunity and why does it matter?
choices: When all cows in a herd are immune to a disease
When a high proportion of a population is vaccinated, preventing disease spread and protecting those who cannot be vaccinated (infants, immunocompromised)
When a disease naturally dies out without any intervention
When vaccines are given to livestock only
questions.explanation: Herd immunity protects vulnerable individuals (newborns, cancer patients, organ transplant recipients) who cannot receive vaccines. If enough people are immune, the pathogen has no 'chain' of susceptible hosts to spread through.

questions.stem: What is the role of memory lymphocytes in the immune response?
choices: They produce toxins that kill all pathogens immediately
They remain in the body for years and enable a rapid, strong antibody response if the same pathogen invades again — this is immunity
They transport oxygen around the body
They digest food in the stomach
questions.explanation: Following an infection or vaccination, memory B and T cells remain dormant. On re-exposure to the same pathogen, they rapidly multiply and produce large quantities of antibodies — often eliminating the pathogen before symptoms appear.

questions.stem: Which lifestyle factor has the strongest direct link to lung cancer?
choices: Eating too much sugar
Not exercising enough
Smoking tobacco
Drinking alcohol
questions.explanation: Tobacco smoke contains over 70 known carcinogens. Smoking causes approximately 85% of lung cancer cases. Tar damages the cilia and lung tissue; carcinogens directly mutate DNA in lung cells.

questions.stem: How does stomach acid act as a defence against pathogens?
choices: It physically washes pathogens out of the stomach
It has a very low pH (~1-2) that denatures pathogen proteins and kills most ingested bacteria
It contains antibodies that neutralise pathogens
It absorbs pathogens into the stomach wall
questions.explanation: Hydrochloric acid in the stomach creates an extremely acidic environment (pH 1-2). This low pH denatures the proteins of most bacteria and pathogens — very few can survive passage through the stomach.

questions.stem: Why is a secondary immune response (2nd exposure) faster and stronger than the primary response (1st exposure)?
choices: The pathogen is weaker the second time
Memory lymphocytes from the first exposure are already present and ready — they rapidly multiply and produce antibodies before the pathogen can establish infection
The body produces more phagocytes the second time
Antibiotics from the first infection remain in the blood
questions.explanation: During the primary response, it takes days for lymphocytes to recognise the antigen, activate, and produce antibodies. Memory cells generated then remain. On re-exposure, they respond within hours — producing a much faster, larger antibody response.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a non-communicable disease?
choices: COVID-19
Malaria
Type 2 diabetes
Tuberculosis
questions.explanation: Type 2 diabetes is largely caused by lifestyle factors (obesity, poor diet, lack of exercise) and genetics. It is NOT contagious. COVID-19 is viral, malaria is a protist, and TB is bacterial — all communicable.

questions.stem: In a practical, agar plates are incubated at 25°C rather than 37°C. Why?
choices: Bacteria grow faster at 25°C
25°C is room temperature so no incubator is needed
Incubating at 37°C (human body temperature) would selectively encourage the growth of human pathogens, creating a significant safety risk in a school laboratory
Bacteria die at 37°C
questions.explanation: Pathogens adapted to the human body thrive at 37°C. In a school setting, incubating at 25°C reduces the risk of accidentally culturing dangerous human pathogens while still allowing safe bacterial species to grow.
